name: Liberia
summary: Founded in 1822 as a settlement for freed African Americans, independent in 1847 — Africa’s oldest republic. Civil wars (1989–2003) ended with Africa’s first elected woman president.

knownFor.label: Ellen Johnson Sirleaf
knownFor.note: First elected woman head of state in Africa.

knownFor.label: Flag of convenience
knownFor.note: Many of the world’s ships are registered here.

location.value: West Africa on the Atlantic; 111,370 km².

terrain.value: A flat coastal plain with lagoons and mangroves, rising to forested hills and the Nimba Mountains in the north, crossed by rivers such as the St Paul.

climate.value: Hot and humid tropical climate with a long rainy season from about May to October; Monrovia is one of the wettest capitals in the world.

resources.value: Rubber from the Firestone plantation (from 1926), iron ore from the Bong and Nimba ranges, timber, gold and diamonds.

disasters.value: Seasonal floods in Monrovia and coastal erosion at places like West Point; the Ebola epidemic of 2014–16 was its worst recent crisis.

urbanisation.value: Monrovia, the capital and main port, holds about a third of the population; other towns include Gbarnga, Buchanan and Harper.

disease.value: The Ebola epidemic of 2014–16 killed nearly 5,000 people in Liberia; malaria remains a leading cause of illness.

economicBase.value: Exports of rubber, iron ore, gold and timber, plus fees from its ship registry, one of the largest in the world.

tradeRoutes.value: Iron ore, rubber and gold leave through the Freeport of Monrovia and Buchanan; many foreign ships fly the Liberian flag.

wealth.value: A low-income country, among the poorest after the civil wars, though iron ore and rubber brought fast growth in the 1950s–70s.

moneyAndTax.value: The Liberian dollar and the US dollar are both used; government revenue comes from taxes, mining and shipping registry fees.

inequality.value: Large gaps between the capital and rural areas.

governmentType.value: A presidential republic modelled on the US.

keyRulers.value: Joseph Jenkins Roberts. William Tubman. Samuel Doe. Charles Taylor. Ellen Johnson Sirleaf.

succession.value: Presidents are elected for six-year terms with a two-term limit; the 2018 handover was the first peaceful transfer between elected presidents since 1944.

institutions.value: A legislature of a Senate and House of Representatives, an elected president, the Supreme Court, and a constitution adopted in 1986.

stability.value: Coup of 12 April 1980 (Samuel Doe); civil wars 1989–2003.

eliteConflict.value: Competition between political parties and leaders.

armyAndTech.value: The Armed Forces of Liberia were disbanded and rebuilt from 2005 with US help; UN peacekeepers (UNMIL) stayed from 2003 to 2018.

majorWars.value: Liberian civil wars (1989–2003): about 250,000 deaths, roughly 8% of the population.

territoryChange.value: Lost claimed lands to British Sierra Leone and to French Guinea and Ivory Coast in boundary treaties of the late 1800s and early 1900s.

alliancesRivals.value: Close ties to the United States, which recognised it in 1862; a founding member of the UN (1945), the OAU (1963) and ECOWAS (1975).

inventions.value: No major inventions are associated with the modern state.

scienceEducation.value: The University of Liberia (founded as Liberia College in 1862), Cuttington University, and schools rebuilt after the civil wars.

openness.value: Open to trade and foreign investment, with periods of restriction.

communicationTransport.value: Roads, many unpaved, link Monrovia to the interior; railways carried iron ore from the Nimba and Bong mines to the coast.

religion.value: Mostly Christian (about 85%), with a Muslim minority of about 12% and some followers of traditional beliefs.

languageWriting.value: English is official, and Liberian English is widely spoken, along with Kpelle, Bassa, Grebo and other languages; the Vai have their own script (1830s).

artsArchitecture.value: Carved wooden masks of the Dan and of the Poro and Sande societies, textiles, and American-style settler houses in towns such as Monrovia.

sharedIdentity.value: A national identity rebuilt after the civil wars, bringing together Americo-Liberians and the country’s 16 ethnic groups.

dailyLife.value: Rice is the main food, with cassava, palm oil and fish; many people live in zinc-roofed houses and work in farming or trade.

neighbours.value: Sierra Leone to the west, Guinea to the north, and Ivory Coast (Côte d’Ivoire) to the east, with the Atlantic Ocean to the south.

ideasReligions.value: Christianity brought by settlers and missionaries, the Poro and Sande initiation societies, and Islam among the Mandingo and Vai.

colonisation.value: Never colonised by a European power, though it lost land to Britain and France and relied on US backing and Firestone investment.

riseSignals.value: Declared independence on 26 July 1847; the United States recognised it on 5 February 1862.

peakPeriod.value: Too recent to judge; the Tubman years (1944–71) brought fast growth from iron ore and rubber, though gains went mainly to the elite.

declineSignals.value: The 1980 coup and the civil wars of 1989–97 and 1999–2003, which wrecked the economy and killed around 250,000 people.

outcome.value: Still an independent republic, at peace since 2003, with UN peacekeepers withdrawn in 2018.

overallCertainty.value: Basic facts are well documented; some figures are estimates.
